items.text: The payment pipeline already has strong transactional foundations: webhook idempotency via stripe_event_id unique constraints, row-level locking on credit wallets, atomic email migration across all tables, and normalized email lookups. These mean guardrails should focus on detection and recovery, not adding more transactional safety.

Structured logging exists for all critical payment events (checkout_session_created, webhook_processing_failed, credits_consumed, etc.) via logStructured()/logStructuredError(), but there is no aggregation, alerting, or dashboard infrastructure consuming these logs.

The highest-risk reconciliation gap is checkout-to-subscription: if Stripe webhook delivery fails after retries, a user has paid but has no subscription record. The checkout_sessions table records the session but nothing periodically checks for paid-but-not-fulfilled sessions.
Download fulfillment returns presigned S3 URLs but does not track whether the user actually completed the download. Failed downloads after authorization are invisible to operators.

items.context: The description lists 5 areas: anomaly alerting, reconciliation, failed fulfillment signals, manual recovery hooks, and dashboards. These range from lightweight (add a reconciliation cron job) to heavyweight (build admin dashboards). For a research item, we need to decide how broad vs. deep the recommendations should be.

options.label: Full breadth — cover all 5 areas with concrete recommendations for each
options.rationale: Produces a comprehensive guardrail plan ready to generate multiple execution items

options.label: Prioritized depth — focus on the 2-3 highest-risk areas with detailed designs
options.rationale: Produces deeper, more actionable recommendations but may leave gaps

items.context: The checkout-to-subscription gap is the highest-risk scenario. There are two main approaches to reconciliation: proactive (periodic job that checks Stripe API against local state) or reactive (enhanced webhook error handling with dead-letter queue and retry).

options.label: Periodic reconciliation job — cron that queries Stripe API to find paid sessions missing local subscriptions
options.rationale: Catches all failure modes (missed webhooks, partial writes, bugs) but adds Stripe API calls and a scheduler dependency

options.label: Enhanced webhook pipeline — dead-letter queue for failed webhook processing with automated retry and manual review
options.rationale: Lower latency for webhook-specific failures but doesn't catch non-webhook gaps

options.label: Both — belt and suspenders
options.rationale: Maximum coverage but more implementation effort

items.context: LPBS already emits structured logs but has no alerting. The question is what infrastructure to recommend for consuming these logs and generating alerts. This affects the complexity and operational burden of the guardrails.

options.label: In-app alerting — API-level anomaly detection with notifications (email/webhook) when thresholds are breached
options.rationale: Self-contained, no external dependencies, but requires building alert logic and notification delivery

options.label: Stripe-native — rely on Stripe Dashboard alerts for payment anomalies, supplement with basic API health checks
options.rationale: Minimal implementation but limited to what Stripe exposes and doesn't cover fulfillment gaps

options.label: External observability stack — recommend Grafana/Prometheus/Loki or similar for log aggregation and alerting
options.rationale: Industry-standard approach but significant infrastructure overhead for a single scenario

plan_updates: Created initial conclusion.md scaffold with research question, methodology, and 5 initial findings covering transactional foundations, logging gaps, checkout-to-subscription reconciliation risk, download fulfillment visibility, and missing admin tooling.
